← Notebook
PathwayToursHistoryThemesMindmapSearch 1 Quivers and seeds 2 Mutation and the exchange relation 3 The Laurent phenomenon and positivity 4 Finite type and the ADE classification 5 Cluster categories and τ-tilting 6 Grassmannians, surfaces, and total positivity 7 Connections

Cluster algebras

A combinatorial machine, invented by Fomin and Zelevinsky in 2000, that turns a quiver and an $n$-tuple of indeterminates into an unending tree of Laurent polynomials. The recursion looks artificial — until exactly the same tree drops out of triangulations of polygons, of Plücker coordinates on Grassmannians, of Auslander–Reiten quivers in representation theory, and of total positivity in Lie groups. The same combinatorial object explains why all of those phenomena fit together.

blocks.html:
1. Quivers and seeds

Fix a positive integer $n$. A quiver $Q$ is a finite directed multigraph on vertices $\{1,\dots,n\}$ with no loops and no oriented $2$-cycles. The data of $Q$ is captured by an $n\times n$ skew-symmetric integer matrix $B = (b_{ij})$, the exchange matrix: $b_{ij}$ is the number of arrows $i\to j$ minus the number of arrows $j\to i$. Skew-symmetry $b_{ij}=-b_{ji}$ is the no-2-cycle condition.

A seed is a pair $(\mathbf{x},B)$ where $\mathbf{x}=(x_1,\dots,x_n)$ is an $n$-tuple of algebraically independent generators of the rational function field $\mathcal{F}=\mathbb{Q}(x_1,\dots,x_n)$ (the cluster) and $B$ is the exchange matrix. We will draw the quiver with each vertex labelled by its cluster variable $x_i$.

The cluster variables and the quiver carry equal weight. The variables tell you which polynomial generators of $\mathcal{F}$ are currently "in scope"; the quiver tells you how to obtain new generators by mutation. A single seed is one chart of an atlas; the cluster algebra $\mathcal{A}\subset\mathcal{F}$ is generated by all cluster variables of all seeds reachable from the starting one, but each individual seed only knows about its own $n$ variables.

params.bodyScript:
<script>
(function(){
  const svg = document.querySelector('#cl-seed-svg');
  const out = document.querySelector('#cl-seed-out');
  if(!svg || !out) return;
  // Quiver layout: three vertices in a row, two arrows
  const verts = [
    {i:1, x:200, y:90, label:'x₁'},
    {i:2, x:360, y:90, label:'x₂'},
    {i:3, x:520, y:90, label:'x₃'}
  ];
  const arrows = [
    {a:0, b:1, mark:'cl-seed-arr-12'},
    {a:1, b:2, mark:'cl-seed-arr-23'}
  ];
  // exchange matrix B for 1 -> 2 -> 3:
  const B = [[0,1,0],[-1,0,1],[0,-1,0]];

  let highlight = null;

  function render(){
    while(svg.firstChild) svg.removeChild(svg.firstChild);
    // arrows first, then nodes on top
    arrows.forEach(a => {
      const v1 = verts[a.a], v2 = verts[a.b];
      drawArrow(svg, [v1.x, v1.y], [v2.x, v2.y], {
        color:'var(--yellow)', markerId:a.mark, width:2, pad1:24, pad2:24
      });
    });
    verts.forEach((v,idx) => {
      const isHi = highlight === idx;
      const stroke = isHi ? 'var(--cyan)' : 'var(--blue)';
      const fill = isHi ? 'var(--panel2)' : 'var(--panel2)';
      svg.appendChild(SVG('circle',{cx:v.x, cy:v.y, r:24,
        fill, stroke, 'stroke-width':isHi?3:1.5,
        'data-vertex': idx, style:'cursor:pointer'}));
      const t = SVG('text',{x:v.x, y:v.y+5, 'text-anchor':'middle',
        'font-size':16, fill: isHi?'var(--cyan)':'#fff', 'font-weight':600,
        'pointer-events':'none'});
      t.textContent = v.label;
      svg.appendChild(t);
    });
    // exchange matrix on the right
    const mx = 600, my = 30;
    const rowH = 32, colW = 36;
    const t0 = SVG('text',{x:mx, y:my-2, 'font-size':12, fill:'var(--mute)'});
    t0.textContent = 'B =';
    svg.appendChild(t0);
    for(let r=0;r<3;r++){
      for(let c=0;c<3;c++){
        const v = B[r][c];
        const cell = SVG('rect',{x:mx + c*colW, y:my + r*rowH, width:colW-2, height:rowH-2,
          fill: highlight===c ? 'rgba(125,224,214,0.15)' : 'rgba(0,0,0,0.18)',
          stroke: highlight===c ? 'var(--cyan)' : 'var(--line)',
          'stroke-width':1});
        svg.appendChild(cell);
        const tt = SVG('text',{x:mx + c*colW + (colW-2)/2, y:my + r*rowH + rowH/2 + 4,
          'text-anchor':'middle','font-size':14,
          fill: v===0 ? 'var(--mute)' : (v>0?'var(--yellow)':'var(--pink)')});
        tt.textContent = String(v);
        svg.appendChild(tt);
      }
    }
    // row/col labels
    for(let i=0;i<3;i++){
      const lr = SVG('text',{x:mx-12, y:my + i*rowH + rowH/2 + 4, 'text-anchor':'end',
        'font-size':11, fill:'var(--mute)'});
      lr.textContent = String(i+1);
      svg.appendChild(lr);
      const lc = SVG('text',{x:mx + i*colW + (colW-2)/2, y:my-6, 'text-anchor':'middle',
        'font-size':11, fill: highlight===i?'var(--cyan)':'var(--mute)'});
      lc.textContent = String(i+1);
      svg.appendChild(lc);
    }
    // wire click handlers (re-bound after each render)
    svg.querySelectorAll('circle[data-vertex]').forEach(c => {
      c.addEventListener('click', () => {
        const idx = parseInt(c.getAttribute('data-vertex'),10);
        highlight = (highlight === idx) ? null : idx;
        update();
      });
    });
  }

  function update(){
    render();
    if(highlight === null){
      out.textContent = 'Click a vertex (x₁, x₂, or x₃) to highlight its column of B and read the exchange relation that mutation at that vertex would produce.';
      return;
    }
    const k = highlight;
    const col = [B[0][k], B[1][k], B[2][k]];
    const pos = [], neg = [];
    col.forEach((v,i) => {
      if(v>0) pos.push(`x${i+1}^${v}`.replace('^1',''));
      if(v<0) neg.push(`x${i+1}^${-v}`.replace('^1',''));
    });
    const left = pos.length ? pos.join('·') : '1';
    const right = neg.length ? neg.join('·') : '1';
    out.textContent =
      `Vertex ${k+1}: column ${k+1} of B is (${col.join(', ')}).\n` +
      `Mutation μ_${k+1} would give the new variable x'${k+1} with\n` +
      `   x_${k+1} · x'_${k+1} = ${left} + ${right}.`;
  }

  update();
})();
</script>

blocks.html: When the quiver has a 2-cycle $i\rightleftarrows j$ — say $b_{ij}=2,\,b_{ji}=-2$ — the corresponding cluster algebra is also defined, but mutation no longer behaves combinatorially the same way. Banning 2-cycles is the right normalisation: any quiver-with-2-cycles can be reduced to a 2-cycle-free one by absorbing the cycles into multiplicity, which is what the skew-symmetric matrix records.

See also
  • Groups, rings, and fields
  • Polynomial rings and irreducibility

Used in
Cluster algebras · Mutation and the exchange relation
</section>

2. Mutation and the exchange relation

Fix a vertex $k\in\{1,\dots,n\}$. Mutation at $k$ is a transformation $\mu_k\colon (\mathbf{x},B)\mapsto (\mathbf{x}',B')$ defined as follows.

The new cluster $\mathbf{x}'$ replaces only $x_k$, leaving the other entries unchanged: $x_i'=x_i$ for $i\ne k$. The new $x_k'$ satisfies the exchange relation

$$x_k\,x_k' \;=\; \prod_{i:\,b_{ik}>0} x_i^{\,b_{ik}} \;+\; \prod_{i:\,b_{ik}<0} x_i^{\,-b_{ik}}.$$

The new exchange matrix $B'$ is given by the matrix mutation rule:

$$b'_{ij} \;=\; \begin{cases} -b_{ij} & \text{if } i=k \text{ or } j=k,\\ b_{ij} + \dfrac{|b_{ik}|\,b_{kj} + b_{ik}\,|b_{kj}|}{2} & \text{otherwise.}\end{cases}$$

The matrix rule is involutive ($\mu_k(\mu_k(B))=B$) and a short check shows the variable rule is too — so $\mu_k$ is its own inverse and the set of seeds carries an action of the free product of $n$ copies of $\mathbb{Z}/2$.

The simplest example

Take $n=2$ with quiver $1\to 2$, exchange matrix $\begin{pmatrix}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{pmatrix}$, cluster $(x_1,x_2)$. Mutation at $1$:

$$x_1\,x_1' = 1 + x_2,\qquad B' = \begin{pmatrix}0 & -1\\ 1 & 0\end{pmatrix}\;\;(\text{quiver flipped to } 2\to 1).$$

So $x_1' = (1+x_2)/x_1$, and the new seed is $\big((x_1',x_2),\; 2\to 1\big)$. Continue mutating alternately at $1$ then $2$ then $1$, and a remarkable thing happens: after five mutations, you return to the starting seed (with the variables permuted). Type $A_2$ is periodic.

params.bodyScript:
<script>
(function(){
  const svg = document.querySelector('#cl-mut-svg');
  const out = document.querySelector('#cl-mut-out');
  const b1 = document.querySelector('#cl-mut-1');
  const b2 = document.querySelector('#cl-mut-2');
  const br = document.querySelector('#cl-mut-reset');
  if(!svg || !out) return;
  // Pre-computed five seeds of A2 starting at (x1, x2) with quiver 1->2.
  // Mutation alternates direction of the arrow.
  const seeds = [
    {x:['x_1','x_2'],            arrow:'→', label:'(x_1, x_2)'},
    {x:['(1+x_2)/x_1','x_2'],    arrow:'←', label:'((1+x_2)/x_1, x_2)'},
    {x:['(1+x_2)/x_1','(1+x_1+x_2)/(x_1 x_2)'], arrow:'→', label:'((1+x_2)/x_1, (1+x_1+x_2)/(x_1 x_2))'},
    {x:['(1+x_1)/x_2','(1+x_1+x_2)/(x_1 x_2)'], arrow:'←', label:'((1+x_1)/x_2, (1+x_1+x_2)/(x_1 x_2))'},
    {x:['(1+x_1)/x_2','x_1'],    arrow:'→', label:'((1+x_1)/x_2, x_1)'}
  ];
  // Vertices of the pentagon for the seed graph
  const cx = 360, cy = 145, R = 95;
  const pent = [];
  for(let k=0;k<5;k++){
    const ang = -Math.PI/2 + 2*Math.PI*k/5;
    pent.push({x:cx + R*Math.cos(ang), y:cy + R*Math.sin(ang)});
  }
  let cur = 0;

  function draw(){
    while(svg.firstChild) svg.removeChild(svg.firstChild);
    // edges of the pentagon (each is a mutation step)
    for(let k=0;k<5;k++){
      const a = pent[k], b = pent[(k+1)%5];
      const isCur = (cur===k);
      svg.appendChild(SVG('line',{x1:a.x, y1:a.y, x2:b.x, y2:b.y,
        stroke: isCur ? 'var(--yellow)' : 'var(--line)', 'stroke-width': isCur?3:1.4}));
      // label the edge with which vertex was mutated
      const mx = (a.x+b.x)/2, my = (a.y+b.y)/2;
      const lbl = SVG('text',{x:mx + 8*Math.sign(mx-cx)*0.7, y:my + 8*Math.sign(my-cy)*0.7,
        'text-anchor':'middle','font-size':12, fill:'var(--mute)'});
      lbl.textContent = (k%2===0) ? 'μ₁' : 'μ₂';
      svg.appendChild(lbl);
    }
    // pentagon vertices
    pent.forEach((p,k) => {
      const isCur = (k===cur);
      svg.appendChild(SVG('circle',{cx:p.x, cy:p.y, r: isCur?14:10,
        fill: isCur ? 'var(--yellow)' : 'var(--panel2)',
        stroke: isCur ? 'var(--yellow)' : 'var(--blue)', 'stroke-width':2}));
      const t = SVG('text',{x:p.x, y:p.y+4, 'text-anchor':'middle',
        'font-size':12, fill: isCur?'#111':'var(--ink)','font-weight':600});
      t.textContent = String(k+1);
      svg.appendChild(t);
    });
    // legend / current seed
    const lg = SVG('text',{x:24, y:28, 'font-size':13, fill:'var(--mute)'});
    lg.textContent = 'Cluster sequence: each vertex of the pentagon is a seed; each edge is one mutation.';
    svg.appendChild(lg);
  }

  function update(){
    draw();
    const s = seeds[cur];
    out.textContent =
      `Seed #${cur+1}\n` +
      `   cluster:  (${s.x[0]},  ${s.x[1]})\n` +
      `   quiver:   1 ${s.arrow} 2`;
  }

  b1.addEventListener('click', () => {
    // mutate at 1: this is the edge taken at even steps; the arrow points 1->2 there
    cur = (cur + 1) % 5;
    if(cur % 2 === 0) cur = (cur + 4) % 5; // step back if we'd take the wrong edge
    // simplest: alternate buttons; just always advance and see — actually
    // for A2 with this seed labeling, μ1 advances when current arrow is →, μ2 when ←
    // but we want the user to feel both buttons; let's force the rule:
    // (rebuild cur from the button press)
    update();
  });
  // Cleanest impl: just alternate and let either button advance; force 5-cycle.
  b1.replaceWith(b1.cloneNode(true));
  b2.replaceWith(b2.cloneNode(true));
  const nb1 = document.querySelector('#cl-mut-1');
  const nb2 = document.querySelector('#cl-mut-2');
  function step(which){
    const expected = (cur % 2 === 0) ? 1 : 2;
    if(which !== expected){
      out.textContent = `At seed #${cur+1} the next mutation is μ${expected}, not μ${which}. (Mutating at the same vertex twice in a row would just go back where you came from.)`;
      return;
    }
    cur = (cur + 1) % 5;
    update();
  }
  nb1.addEventListener('click', () => step(1));
  nb2.addEventListener('click', () => step(2));
  br.addEventListener('click', () => { cur = 0; update(); });

  update();
})();
</script>

3. The Laurent phenomenon and positivity

Computing a cluster variable directly from the recursion produces an arbitrary rational function in $(x_1,\dots,x_n)$ — a quotient of polynomials with potentially huge denominators. Yet:

Theorem (Fomin–Zelevinsky, 2002). Every cluster variable, after any sequence of mutations, is a Laurent polynomial in the initial cluster $\mathbf{x}=(x_1,\dots,x_n)$. That is, every cluster variable lies in $\mathbb{Z}[x_1^{\pm 1},\dots,x_n^{\pm 1}]$.

This is the Laurent phenomenon. The denominator of any cluster variable, no matter how deep the mutation tree, is always a single monomial in the initial $x_i$'s. For type $A_2$ that is visible directly in the five seeds: $x_3=(1+x_2)/x_1$, $x_4=(1+x_1+x_2)/(x_1x_2)$, $x_5=(1+x_1)/x_2$ — all denominators monomial in $\{x_1,x_2\}$.

Positivity

A stronger conjecture, proved in many cases:

Theorem (Lee–Schiffler 2015 for skew-symmetric type; Gross–Hacking–Keel–Kontsevich 2018 in general). The Laurent polynomials in the previous theorem have non-negative integer coefficients.

So every cluster variable $x = \frac{P(x_1,\dots,x_n)}{x_1^{d_1}\cdots x_n^{d_n}}$ has $P\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}[x_1,\dots,x_n]$. The non-negative integer coefficients are not just a curiosity: they count something — Caldero–Chapoton expressed them as Euler characteristics of quiver Grassmannians, and Gross–Hacking–Keel–Kontsevich realised them as counts of broken lines in scattering diagrams.

blocks.html: The proof of the Laurent phenomenon is a clever induction on the depth of mutation: one shows that any two cluster variables are coprime in the appropriate Laurent ring — so when a new variable is created by exchange, the only $x_i$ that can appear in the denominator is the one being mutated. Positivity is much harder; for ages, the only known cases were the surface-type cluster algebras (where Musiker–Schiffler–Williams gave a manifest formula counting perfect matchings of an associated snake graph).

See also
  • Polynomial rings and irreducibility

Used in
Cluster algebras · Finite type and the ADE classification
</section>

4. Finite type and the ADE classification

Most cluster algebras have infinitely many cluster variables. The exception is when the recursion terminates after finitely many distinct seeds — a finite type cluster algebra.

Theorem (Fomin–Zelevinsky 2003). A cluster algebra has finite type if and only if it has a seed whose quiver, after possibly orienting edges, is a Dynkin diagram of finite type — i.e. one of the simply-laced $A_n$, $D_n$, $E_6$, $E_7$, $E_8$, or (with non-trivial multiplicities permitted) $B_n$, $C_n$, $F_4$, $G_2$.

The number of cluster variables in each finite type matches the count of almost positive roots (positive roots plus negative simple roots) of the corresponding root system. For $A_n$ that count is $n(n+3)/2$. For $E_8$ it is $128$. The cluster algebra contains exactly that many distinct cluster variables, and exactly $\frac{1}{n+2}\binom{2(n+1)}{n+1}=C_{n+1}$ clusters in type $A_n$ — the Catalan numbers.

The polygon model for type $A_n$

For type $A_n$, the cluster combinatorics has a beautiful classical realisation: take a convex $(n+3)$-gon $P_{n+3}$. Then

  • Cluster variables ↔ diagonals of $P_{n+3}$ (sides are frozen variables).
  • Clusters ↔ triangulations of $P_{n+3}$ by non-crossing diagonals.
  • Mutation ↔ flipping one diagonal of a triangulation: the diagonal sits inside a unique quadrilateral and gets replaced by the other diagonal of that quadrilateral.

The number of triangulations of $P_{n+3}$ is the Catalan number $C_{n+1}$, matching the cluster count above. The exchange relation $x_kx_k' = M_+ + M_-$ becomes Ptolemy's theorem for the relevant quadrilateral: the product of the two diagonals equals the sum of products of opposite sides.

params.title: Polygon flip explorer — type $A_n$
params.hint: click a diagonal to flip it to the other diagonal of its quadrilateral
params.bodyMarkup:
Polygon flip explorer — type $A_n$
click a diagonal to flip it to the other diagonal of its quadrilateral
params.bodyScript:
<script>
(function(){
  const svg = document.querySelector('#cl-flip-svg');
  const out = document.querySelector('#cl-flip-out');
  const sel = document.querySelector('#cl-flip-n');
  const rst = document.querySelector('#cl-flip-reset');
  if(!svg || !out) return;

  let n = 3;
  let N = n+3;
  const cx = 360, cy = 180, R = 130;
  // verts and triangulation diagonals as pairs (i,j) with j > i+1
  let verts = [];
  let diags = []; // array of [i,j]
  let flipCount = 0;

  function buildPolygon(){
    N = n+3;
    verts = [];
    for(let k=0;k<N;k++){
      const a = -Math.PI/2 + 2*Math.PI*k/N;
      verts.push({x:cx + R*Math.cos(a), y:cy + R*Math.sin(a)});
    }
    // initial triangulation: fan from vertex 0
    diags = [];
    for(let k=2;k<N-1;k++) diags.push([0,k]);
    flipCount = 0;
  }

  function neighbors(i,j){
    // For diagonal (i,j) in current triangulation, find the two vertices
    // forming the unique quadrilateral with (i,j) as one diagonal.
    // i.e. the two triangles containing (i,j) — find their third vertices.
    // Build adjacency: for each vertex v, the diagonals/sides at v.
    // sides of polygon: (k, (k+1)%N) for all k.
    // We find vertices p,q such that both (i,p) or (p,i) and (j,p) or (p,j)
    // are edges of the triangulation (= diagonals or sides), and p ≠ i,j.
    const isEdge = (a,b) => {
      if(a>b){ const t=a; a=b; b=t; }
      if(b===a+1) return true;            // adjacent on polygon
      if(a===0 && b===N-1) return true;   // wrap-around side
      return diags.some(d => (d[0]===a && d[1]===b) || (d[0]===b && d[1]===a));
    };
    const ps = [];
    for(let p=0;p<N;p++){
      if(p===i || p===j) continue;
      if(isEdge(i,p) && isEdge(j,p)) ps.push(p);
    }
    return ps;
  }

  function flip(idx){
    const [i,j] = diags[idx];
    const ps = neighbors(i,j);
    if(ps.length !== 2) return null;
    const [p,q] = ps;
    // Replace (i,j) with (p,q)
    diags[idx] = [Math.min(p,q), Math.max(p,q)];
    flipCount++;
    return [p,q];
  }

  function render(){
    while(svg.firstChild) svg.removeChild(svg.firstChild);
    // sides of polygon
    for(let k=0;k<N;k++){
      const a = verts[k], b = verts[(k+1)%N];
      svg.appendChild(SVG('line',{x1:a.x, y1:a.y, x2:b.x, y2:b.y,
        stroke:'var(--mute)','stroke-width':1.5}));
    }
    // diagonals (clickable)
    diags.forEach((d, idx) => {
      const a = verts[d[0]], b = verts[d[1]];
      const line = SVG('line',{x1:a.x, y1:a.y, x2:b.x, y2:b.y,
        stroke:'var(--yellow)','stroke-width':2.4,
        'data-d':idx, style:'cursor:pointer'});
      svg.appendChild(line);
      // invisible click target (thicker)
      const hit = SVG('line',{x1:a.x, y1:a.y, x2:b.x, y2:b.y,
        stroke:'transparent','stroke-width':14,
        'data-d':idx, style:'cursor:pointer'});
      svg.appendChild(hit);
    });
    // vertices
    verts.forEach((v,k) => {
      svg.appendChild(SVG('circle',{cx:v.x, cy:v.y, r:6, fill:'var(--blue)'}));
      const t = SVG('text',{x:v.x + 16*Math.cos(-Math.PI/2 + 2*Math.PI*k/N),
        y:v.y + 16*Math.sin(-Math.PI/2 + 2*Math.PI*k/N) + 4,
        'text-anchor':'middle','font-size':12, fill:'var(--mute)'});
      t.textContent = String(k);
      svg.appendChild(t);
    });
    // wire clicks
    svg.querySelectorAll('[data-d]').forEach(el => {
      el.addEventListener('click', () => {
        const idx = parseInt(el.getAttribute('data-d'),10);
        const before = diags[idx].slice();
        const after = flip(idx);
        if(after){
          out.textContent =
            `Flipped diagonal (${before[0]}, ${before[1]}) → (${after[0]}, ${after[1]}).\n` +
            `That's a mutation μ at the cluster variable x(${before[0]}, ${before[1]}).\n` +
            `Total flips so far: ${flipCount}. Remaining diagonals: ${diags.length}.`;
        } else {
          out.textContent = `Diagonal (${before[0]}, ${before[1]}) is on the boundary of the current triangulation — cannot flip (this should not normally happen).`;
        }
        render();
      });
    });
    // status
    const t = SVG('text',{x:24, y:30, 'font-size':13, fill:'var(--mute)'});
    t.textContent = `(n+3)=${N}-gon · ${diags.length} diagonals · cluster size ${diags.length} · type A${n} has ${n*(n+3)/2} cluster variables total`;
    svg.appendChild(t);
  }

  function update(){
    render();
    if(!out.textContent){
      out.textContent =
        `Initial triangulation: fan from vertex 0. Click any yellow diagonal to flip it.\n` +
        `(n+3)=${N}-gon, type A${n}: ${n*(n+3)/2} cluster variables total, ${(function(){
          // C_{n+1} closed form
          let r = 1;
          for(let k=1;k<=n+1;k++) r = r * (n+1+k) / k;
          return Math.round(r/(n+2));
        })()} clusters.`;
    }
  }

  sel.addEventListener('change', () => {
    n = parseInt(sel.value,10);
    buildPolygon();
    out.textContent = '';
    update();
  });
  rst.addEventListener('click', () => {
    buildPolygon();
    out.textContent = '';
    update();
  });

  buildPolygon();
  update();
})();
</script>

blocks.html: The exchange graph of the type-$A_n$ cluster algebra — vertices are clusters, edges are mutations — is the 1-skeleton of the Stasheff associahedron $K_{n+2}$, a convex polytope of dimension $n$ first studied for its role in higher coherence laws of monoidal categories. Cluster algebras hand you a polytope. Conversely, the higher exceptional types $E_{6,7,8}$ produce $42$, $70$, $128$ cluster variables and exotic exchange polytopes that have no surface model — they are visible only through the abstract Dynkin combinatorics.

See also
  • Cartan, Killing, and semisimplicity

Used in
Cluster algebras · Cluster categories and τ-tilting
</section>

5. Cluster categories and τ-tilting

The combinatorial recursion of mutation looked like an isolated trick until categorification caught up. For a Dynkin quiver $Q$, Buan–Marsh–Reineke–Reiten–Todorov defined the cluster category as an orbit category of the bounded derived category of finite-dimensional $kQ$-modules:

$$\mathcal{C}_Q \;:=\; D^b(\mathrm{mod}\,kQ)\;\big/\;\tau^{-1}\circ[1].$$

Here $\tau$ is the Auslander–Reiten translation and $[1]$ is the suspension. Keller proved that this orbit category is again triangulated, and moreover $2$-Calabi–Yau: there is a functorial duality $\mathrm{Ext}^1_{\mathcal{C}}(X,Y) \cong D\,\mathrm{Ext}^1_{\mathcal{C}}(Y,X)$.

The dictionary BMRRT established is striking:

Cluster algebra sideCluster category side
Cluster variableIndecomposable rigid object ($\mathrm{Ext}^1(X,X)=0$)
Cluster (= seed)Cluster-tilting object $T = T_1\oplus\cdots\oplus T_n$
Mutation $\mu_k$Iyama–Yoshino exchange: replace $T_k$ by the unique other $T_k^*$ giving a cluster-tilting object
Exchange relationTwo non-split exchange triangles $T_k^*\to E\to T_k\to T_k^*[1]$
Laurent expansion (Caldero–Chapoton)$\sum_e \chi(\mathrm{Gr}_e(M))\prod x_i^{\langle\dim,\beta_i\rangle}$

The Caldero–Chapoton formula expresses the Laurent polynomial expansion of a cluster variable as a generating function over Euler characteristics of quiver Grassmannians — geometric loci parametrising submodules of a fixed dimension vector. The positive integer coefficients of the Laurent expansion are then manifestly Euler characteristics of complex algebraic varieties, hence non-negative integers. This was the first proof of positivity in the surface case and remains a central tool.

<script>
(function(){
  const svg = document.querySelector('#cl-arq-svg');
  const out = document.querySelector('#cl-arq-out');
  if(!svg || !out) return;
  // 9 indecomposables of the A3 cluster category, arranged as the AR quiver
  // organised as 3 columns x 3 rows. Each indecomposable corresponds to a
  // diagonal of the hexagon (n=3, hexagon = 6-gon).
  // We use the standard correspondence: indecomposables are labeled by
  // arcs/diagonals of the hexagon (vertices 0..5).
  const indec = [
    {x:120, y:80,  label:'M₁',   diag:[0,2], desc:'simple S₁; arc (0,2)'},
    {x:120, y:170, label:'M₃',   diag:[0,4], desc:'projective P₁; arc (0,4)'},
    {x:120, y:260, label:'M₅',   diag:[0,3], desc:'P[1]; arc (0,3)'},
    {x:340, y:80,  label:'M₂',   diag:[1,3], desc:'simple S₂; arc (1,3)'},
    {x:340, y:170, label:'M₄',   diag:[1,5], desc:'projective P₂; arc (1,5)'},
    {x:340, y:260, label:'M₆',   diag:[1,4], desc:'M[1]; arc (1,4)'},
    {x:560, y:80,  label:'M₇',   diag:[2,4], desc:'simple S₃; arc (2,4)'},
    {x:560, y:170, label:'M₈',   diag:[3,5], desc:'projective P₃; arc (3,5)'},
    {x:560, y:260, label:'M₉',   diag:[2,5], desc:'P[1]; arc (2,5)'}
  ];
  // AR translate: roughly shift right one column (with wrap)
  // For visualisation we draw arrows between adjacent columns.
  const arrows = [
    [0,3],[3,6],[1,4],[4,7],[2,5],[5,8],
    [3,1],[6,4],[4,2],[7,5]
  ];
  // hexagon for the right-side preview
  const hx = 640, hy = 160, hr = 50;
  const hex = [];
  for(let k=0;k<6;k++){
    const a = -Math.PI/2 + 2*Math.PI*k/6;
    hex.push({x:hx + hr*Math.cos(a), y:hy + hr*Math.sin(a)});
  }

  let highlight = null;

  function render(){
    while(svg.firstChild) svg.removeChild(svg.firstChild);
    // arrows
    arrows.forEach(([a,b], idx) => {
      const v1 = indec[a], v2 = indec[b];
      drawArrow(svg, [v1.x, v1.y], [v2.x, v2.y], {
        color:'var(--line)', markerId:'arq-arr-'+idx, width:1.2, pad1:24, pad2:24
      });
    });
    // tau-translation arrows (dashed) — hint at the orbit structure
    // (kept light; main structure is enough)
    // nodes
    indec.forEach((m, idx) => {
      const isHi = highlight === idx;
      svg.appendChild(SVG('circle',{cx:m.x, cy:m.y, r:22,
        fill: isHi?'var(--yellow)':'var(--panel2)',
        stroke: isHi?'var(--yellow)':'var(--blue)',
        'stroke-width':isHi?3:1.5,
        'data-mod':idx, style:'cursor:pointer'}));
      const t = SVG('text',{x:m.x, y:m.y+5, 'text-anchor':'middle',
        'font-size':14, fill:isHi?'#111':'#fff', 'font-weight':600,
        'pointer-events':'none'});
      t.textContent = m.label;
      svg.appendChild(t);
    });
    // wire mouseover
    svg.querySelectorAll('[data-mod]').forEach(el => {
      el.addEventListener('mouseover', () => {
        highlight = parseInt(el.getAttribute('data-mod'),10);
        renderRight();
        update();
      });
      el.addEventListener('mouseout', () => {
        highlight = null;
        renderRight();
        update();
      });
    });
    renderRight();
  }
  function renderRight(){
    // remove old hexagon previews
    svg.querySelectorAll('.hex-preview').forEach(e => e.remove());
    const g = SVG('g',{class:'hex-preview'});
    // outline the hexagon
    for(let k=0;k<6;k++){
      const a = hex[k], b = hex[(k+1)%6];
      g.appendChild(SVG('line',{x1:a.x, y1:a.y, x2:b.x, y2:b.y,
        stroke:'var(--mute)','stroke-width':1}));
    }
    hex.forEach((v,k) => {
      g.appendChild(SVG('circle',{cx:v.x, cy:v.y, r:3, fill:'var(--blue)'}));
      const t = SVG('text',{x:v.x + 12*Math.cos(-Math.PI/2 + 2*Math.PI*k/6),
        y:v.y + 12*Math.sin(-Math.PI/2 + 2*Math.PI*k/6) + 3,
        'text-anchor':'middle','font-size':10, fill:'var(--mute)'});
      t.textContent = String(k);
      g.appendChild(t);
    });
    if(highlight !== null){
      const m = indec[highlight];
      const a = hex[m.diag[0]], b = hex[m.diag[1]];
      g.appendChild(SVG('line',{x1:a.x, y1:a.y, x2:b.x, y2:b.y,
        stroke:'var(--yellow)','stroke-width':2.5}));
    }
    const t = SVG('text',{x:hx, y:hy+hr+24, 'text-anchor':'middle','font-size':11, fill:'var(--mute)'});
    t.textContent = 'hexagon model';
    g.appendChild(t);
    svg.appendChild(g);
  }
  function update(){
    if(highlight === null){
      out.textContent =
        `9 indecomposable objects of the type-A₃ cluster category. ` +
        `The 9 indecomposables match the n(n+3)/2 = 9 diagonals of the hexagon (n=3). ` +
        `Hover any node to see which diagonal it represents.`;
    } else {
      const m = indec[highlight];
      out.textContent =
        `${m.label}: ${m.desc}\n` +
        `corresponds to diagonal (${m.diag[0]}, ${m.diag[1]}) of the hexagon.`;
    }
  }
  render();
  update();
})();
</script>

6. Grassmannians, surfaces, and total positivity

The genuinely surprising payoff is that cluster algebras are everywhere they have any business being. Three first-rank examples.

The Grassmannian $\mathrm{Gr}(2,n)$ and Plücker coordinates

The Grassmannian $\mathrm{Gr}(2,n)$ of $2$-planes in $\mathbb{C}^n$ has homogeneous coordinate ring generated by the Plücker coordinates $p_{ij}$ (with $1\le i<j\le n$), subject to the Plücker relations

$$p_{ik}\,p_{j\ell} \;=\; p_{ij}\,p_{k\ell} \;+\; p_{i\ell}\,p_{jk}\qquad (1\le i<j<k<\ell\le n).$$

These are the same relations one gets by writing exchange relations on the cluster algebra of type $A_{n-3}$ realised by triangulations of an $n$-gon: each $p_{ij}$ corresponds to the chord (or side) of the $n$-gon from vertex $i$ to vertex $j$. The $n$ side-coordinates $p_{i,i+1}$ are frozen (mutate to themselves); the $n(n-3)/2$ diagonal coordinates are mutable cluster variables. Triangulations are the maximal sets of pairwise non-crossing chords — exactly the clusters.

<script>
(function(){
  const svg = document.querySelector('#cl-gr-svg');
  const out = document.querySelector('#cl-gr-out');
  const sel = document.querySelector('#cl-gr-n');
  if(!svg || !out) return;
  let n = 6;
  let verts = [];
  let lastClick = null;
  const cx=360, cy=180, R=130;

  function buildPoly(){
    verts = [];
    for(let k=0;k<n;k++){
      const a = -Math.PI/2 + 2*Math.PI*k/n;
      verts.push({x:cx + R*Math.cos(a), y:cy + R*Math.sin(a)});
    }
  }
  function isFrozen(i,j){
    return ((j-i)===1) || (i===0 && j===n-1);
  }
  function render(){
    while(svg.firstChild) svg.removeChild(svg.firstChild);
    // header
    const hdr = SVG('text',{x:24, y:28, 'font-size':13, fill:'var(--mute)'});
    hdr.textContent = `Gr(2,${n}): ${n} frozen sides + ${n*(n-3)/2} mutable diagonals = ${n*(n-1)/2} total Plückers (type A${n-3}).`;
    svg.appendChild(hdr);
    // sides (frozen)
    for(let k=0;k<n;k++){
      const a = verts[k], b = verts[(k+1)%n];
      svg.appendChild(SVG('line',{x1:a.x, y1:a.y, x2:b.x, y2:b.y,
        stroke:'var(--cyan)','stroke-width':2.4,
        'data-i':k,'data-j':(k+1)%n, style:'cursor:pointer'}));
      const hit = SVG('line',{x1:a.x, y1:a.y, x2:b.x, y2:b.y,
        stroke:'transparent','stroke-width':14,
        'data-i':k,'data-j':(k+1)%n, style:'cursor:pointer'});
      svg.appendChild(hit);
    }
    // diagonals (mutable, dashed)
    for(let i=0;i<n;i++){
      for(let j=i+2;j<n;j++){
        if(i===0 && j===n-1) continue;
        const a = verts[i], b = verts[j];
        svg.appendChild(SVG('line',{x1:a.x, y1:a.y, x2:b.x, y2:b.y,
          stroke:'var(--yellow)','stroke-width':1.6,
          'stroke-dasharray':'4 3',
          'data-i':i,'data-j':j, style:'cursor:pointer'}));
        const hit = SVG('line',{x1:a.x, y1:a.y, x2:b.x, y2:b.y,
          stroke:'transparent','stroke-width':14,
          'data-i':i,'data-j':j, style:'cursor:pointer'});
        svg.appendChild(hit);
      }
    }
    // verts
    verts.forEach((v,k) => {
      svg.appendChild(SVG('circle',{cx:v.x, cy:v.y, r:5, fill:'var(--blue)'}));
      const t = SVG('text',{x:v.x + 14*Math.cos(-Math.PI/2 + 2*Math.PI*k/n),
        y:v.y + 14*Math.sin(-Math.PI/2 + 2*Math.PI*k/n) + 4,
        'text-anchor':'middle','font-size':12, fill:'var(--mute)'});
      t.textContent = String(k+1);
      svg.appendChild(t);
    });
    // wire clicks
    svg.querySelectorAll('[data-i]').forEach(el => {
      el.addEventListener('click', () => {
        const i = parseInt(el.getAttribute('data-i'),10);
        const j = parseInt(el.getAttribute('data-j'),10);
        const lo = Math.min(i,j), hi = Math.max(i,j);
        lastClick = [lo+1, hi+1];
        update();
      });
    });
  }
  function update(){
    render();
    if(lastClick === null){
      out.textContent =
        `Click any chord. Solid cyan = side (frozen Plücker $p_{i,i+1}$). Dashed yellow = diagonal (mutable Plücker).\n` +
        `Number of triangulations of the ${n}-gon = ${(function(){
          // C_{n-2}
          let r=1; for(let k=1;k<=n-2;k++) r=r*(n-2+k)/k; return Math.round(r/(n-1));
        })()} = number of clusters in this Gr(2,${n}) cluster algebra.`;
    } else {
      const [a,b] = lastClick;
      const i = a-1, j = b-1;
      const frozen = ((b-a)===1) || (a===1 && b===n);
      out.textContent =
        `Plücker coordinate p_{${a},${b}}\n` +
        (frozen
          ? `→ this is a side of the ${n}-gon, so p_{${a},${b}} is FROZEN: every cluster contains it.`
          : `→ this is a diagonal of the ${n}-gon, so p_{${a},${b}} is MUTABLE: it lies in some clusters and not others.`);
    }
  }
  sel.addEventListener('change', () => {
    n = parseInt(sel.value,10);
    buildPoly();
    lastClick = null;
    update();
  });
  buildPoly();
  update();
})();
</script>

Bordered surfaces and Teichmüller theory

Fomin–Shapiro–Thurston extended the polygon picture to cluster algebras from surfaces: pick a compact oriented surface $\Sigma$ with marked points on the boundary, plus possibly punctures. Triangulations of $\Sigma$ become clusters; flips of arcs become mutations. The Plücker-style exchange relations recover the lambda-length identities of decorated Teichmüller theory (Penner's work), and one recovers all surface-type cluster algebras simultaneously. Beyond the polygon (= disc with boundary), one gets the annulus, the once-punctured torus, the four-punctured sphere — and infinitely many more.

Total positivity

An $n\times n$ matrix is totally positive if all its minors are positive. Lusztig identified the totally positive part of $\mathrm{GL}_n$ (and more generally, semisimple Lie groups) with a piece carrying a natural cell decomposition; Fomin–Zelevinsky showed the cells are precisely cluster charts, and the cluster variables are the natural functions to test positivity on. This explains why total positivity has the strange "you only need to check a small number of minors" property — the small number is exactly the rank of an appropriate cluster algebra.

Scattering diagrams and the rest

Cluster transformations turn out to be the wall-crossing automorphisms of certain scattering diagrams in the sense of Kontsevich–Soibelman; this perspective, developed by Gross–Hacking–Keel–Kontsevich, gave the proof of positivity in full generality and a canonical basis (theta basis) for cluster algebras. The same combinatorics also organises Donaldson–Thomas theory of quivers, the spectra of supersymmetric quantum field theories (BPS states), and the symbol alphabets of multi-loop scattering amplitudes.

See also
  • Moduli problems and parameters
  • Homogeneous equations and charts
  • The upper half-plane model
</section>

Connections

Cluster algebras began as a combinatorial tool for studying total positivity and Lusztig's canonical bases of quantum groups. Twenty-five years on, the same recursive datum sits at the centre of: representation theory of finite-dimensional algebras (cluster categories, τ-tilting, additive categorification); higher Teichmüller theory (Fock–Goncharov coordinates); mirror symmetry (theta functions, Gross–Hacking–Keel–Kontsevich); and the symbology of scattering amplitudes in $\mathcal{N}=4$ super-Yang–Mills (Drummond–Foster–Gürdoğan). Many of the basic conjectures — positivity, the strong cluster duality of GHKK, the structure of infinite-type cluster algebras — are settled or close to it; the open frontier is now in the direction of generalised cluster structures (cyclic surfaces, higher rank), and applications outside pure math.

  • Quantum groups — $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_n)$ — Lusztig's canonical bases were the original motivation; cluster algebras quantise to give the quantum cluster algebras of Berenstein–Zelevinsky.
  • Representation theory — categorification via cluster categories ties cluster combinatorics to Auslander–Reiten theory and τ-tilting.
  • Derived categories — the cluster category $\mathcal{C}_Q = D^b/\tau^{-1}[1]$ is the natural triangulated home of the BMRRT dictionary.
  • Mirror symmetry — Gross–Hacking–Keel–Kontsevich's scattering-diagram proof of positivity is one half of a homological-mirror-symmetry-style construction for log Calabi–Yau pairs.
  • Moduli spaces — the cluster structure on $\mathrm{Gr}(k,n)$ is the prototype; cluster structures on flag varieties, double Bruhat cells, and moduli of decorated local systems all follow the same script.
